title: Book Review of Yingjin Zhang’s Chinese National Cinema (2004)
text:
Yingjin Zhang’s Chinese National Cinema (2004) was a pioneering text in Anglophone Chinese film studies scholarship. Magisterial in scope, the book is structured as a survey of the institutional and cultural history of mainland Chinese, Taiwanese, and Hong Kong cinemas from the silent era to the present. Aside from the copious references to industry developments and contemporary film criticism drawn from Chinese film history archives (e.g. Zhongguo dianying ziliaoguan, Zhongguo dianying yishu yanjiu zhongxin), Zhang also weaves in short summaries and analyses of key film texts in each period, often citing and introducing the works of present-day Chinese, Taiwanese, and Hong Kong critics. Investigating the three ‘Chinese’ cinemas as distinct evolving “constructions of the national,” he draws comparisons between the role of cinema in the development of Chinese, Taiwanese, and Hong Kong cultural identities. The book has long become a classic reference for scholars in Chinese film studies. Two decades in hindsight, it is not difficult to identify many clues and theses therein that have served as inspiration for other newer scholarship that have appeared since.
Chapter two follows the development of Chinese cinema from its inception to the end of the 1920s. Zhang points out that the earliest films were opera recordings and comedy shorts, which were then subsequently followed by family dramas and urban romances in the first decade of feature films. By the late 1920s, costume dramas, martial arts films, and films of immortals and demons rose to popularity. Zhang argues that the victories of the martial hero and the superstitious tales reflect the desire of the public to escape the surrounding chaos of domestic strife and imperial aggression. Commenting on the theory of Chinese film as “shadowplay” propounded by recent PRC film scholarship, Zhang cautions against hastily positing an indigenous Chinese film aesthetics. Noting that cross-pollination between theater and film is not unique to China but also found in early Western cinema, Zhang argues that the operatic mode of Chinese film is best understood as a convenient strategy to facilitate the initial adoption of cinema technology, rather than the grounds for a unique Chinese film aesthetics.
Chapter three surveys ideological strife and institutional restructurings in Shanghai and the hinterlands during the pre-war and wartime periods. In the 1930s, Zhang proposes that the main cinematic form was political melodrama, which survey social problems while articulating ideal moral visions. During this period, leftist scriptwriters cooperated with existing studios to produce social films like Spring Silkworms (Chuncan, dir. Cheng Bugao, 1933). KMT censors sought to stamp out leftist agendas in films, but only with limited success. The pre-war period also coincided with the transition to sound film and the enforcement of Mandarin dialogue in films, which meant scriptwriters and actors had to learn to write and act in the new vernacular. In the urban landscapes of 1930s family dramas and social films, Zhang observes that suffering women figures serve as sites for mediating national anxiety in the face of sweeping social changes and imperial aggression. After the Japanese occupation of Shanghai in 1937, high inflation and colonial censorship led studios to make cheap, low quality entertainment films. However, Zhang notes that there was an unlikely “second commercial wave” that produced successful films like Confucius (Kongfuzi, dir. Fei Mu, 1940). In the postwar years prior to 1949, Zhang identifies a short-lived trend of films that emphasized humanistic and artistic values such as Fei Mu’s Spring in a Small Town (Xiaocunzhichun, 1948). Intent on establishing the institutional contours of exhibition, production, and consumption, Zhang often overlooks the artistic and cultural effects of film. Particularly in the first two chapters, even though summary statements on stylistic and thematic trends are duly provided, industry history of film exhibition and production overshadow close film analysis and media archaeology.
Chapters four and five study the development of Hong Kong and Taiwan cinema in the first three decades of the postwar era (1945-78). In colonial Taiwan, Japanese films dominated the Taiwanese market and locally produced feature films were scarce. After the KMT takeover, state run studios produced policy films that exposed CCP brutality and praised KMT accomplishments. However, starting with Xue Pinggui and Wang Baochuan (Xue Pinggui he Wang Baochuan, dir. He Jiming, 1956), Zhang notes that the Taiwanese local dialect films (Taiyupian) became increasingly popular throughout the 1950s, overshadowing the anti-communist policy films. In the 1960s, a Hong Kong production The Love Eterne (Liang Shanbo yu Zhu Yingtai, dir. Li Hanxiang, 1963) set off a huge craze in Taiwan. A new venture, Guolian, brought Li Hanxiang to Taiwan to continue producing big budget costume dramas. This company would also oversee multiple film adaptations of Qiong Yao love stories that would take over 1970s Taiwan. Zhang interprets the melodrama of Taiwanese dialect films as an alternative imagination of the national in competition with the heroic narratives of KMT policy films. He also argues that the epic costume dramas and Qiong Yao films of the 1960s and 70s display a strategic escapism that responds to the precarious diplomatic and geopolitical status of the ROC. Although Zhang nicely illustrates the competitive dynamics between Taiwanese local dialect films and KMT policy films, it remains rather unclear why this competition should be understood as a struggle for defining alternate visions of “the national.”
Zhang demonstrates that Hong Kong cinema in the 1950s and 60s was marked by competition between two large studios—Cathay and Shaw Brothers. Starting with Our Sister Hedy (Siqianjin, dir. Tao Qin, 1957), Cathay productions were often urban comedies that highlighted bourgeois lifestyles and youth culture. Its competitor, Shaw Brothers, instead were known for big-budget costume dramas, including Li Hanxiang’s The Love Eterne. Zhang argues that the migration of Mandarin-speaking film producers from Shanghai created the conditions for such Mandarin productions, before the precipitous decline of Mandarin films in the 1970s. Nevertheless, he hastens to add that opera and musical films adapted from both Cantonese and non-Cantonese sources were the most popular. After the riots of 1967, Hong Kong cinema was proliferated with youth idol romances and soft porn. Shortly after, Hong Kong cinema faced a crisis as film productions dropped to zero. Zhang argues that soft porn and youth idol pictures reflect a general mood of “nihilism, disillusionment, and paranoia” in post-riot Hong Kong. Throughout the book, his analysis of film genres chiefly concerns their significance as signs of particular historical moments, thereby largely neglecting the participatory or causative potential of film media. Zhang notes that, in the 1970s, martial arts films revived the industry, replacing opera films as the main genre of Hong Kong cinema. Rounding out his discussion of postwar Hong Kong cinema, Zhang concludes by proposing that Hong Kong cinema embodies a cross-pollination of cultures from different origins, embodying a unique regional imagination.
Chapter six follows the development of socialist cinema from the Communist nationalization of film industry up to the beginning of reform and opening. Zhang points out that, in socialist Chinese cinema, film production coalesced around the party line represented by “Yan’an trained, rural educated cadres.” Socialist realism sought to purge moral ambiguity through establishing clear contrasts between good and bad types. This tendency reached new heights in the model play films of the Cultural Revolution, which Zhang characterizes as full-blown “revolutionary romanticism” without any concern for realism. Building on Dai Jinhua’s thesis about the interpellation of the audience into revolutionary subjects, Zhang further suggests that the third generation of filmmakers were “feminized because they were perceived as subordinate to the masses . . . and their political loyalty was always in doubt.” The full implication of this insight could be made clearer if Zhang elaborated the broader intellectual contexts of Dai Jinhua and his own interventions.
Chapter seven compares New Wave cinemas in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and mainland China. Sinophone cinemas. Zhang observes that mainland Chinese fourth and fifth generation directors experimented with avant-garde film techniques to overcome the drama-centric style of predecessors. For Taiwan New Wave, Zhang identifies two tendencies: the rediscovery of native soil as a repository of local histories and the city as an alienated topoi in which individuals search for their lost identity. Unlike mainland China and Taiwan, Zhang argues that Hong Kong New Wave pictures were not auteur films, but rather commercially viable small-scale productions with mixed-genre elements. Chapter eight discusses the cosmopolitan transregional imagination emerging in Hong Kong and Taiwanese auteurs like Ang Lee and Wong Kar-wai.
Emphasizing the resonances between the New Wave in the three locales, these final chapters are a fitting conclusion to the earlier chapters’ immensely informative, yet relatively separate, histories of mainland Chinese, Taiwanese, and Hong Kong cinemas. The final two chapters come closest to directly comparing the different cinematic constructions of the national (or political community) in the three locales. However, the only major point of similarity noted between fifth generation Chinese cinema and New Taiwan Cinema are that they are both situated in contra-position to commercial and propaganda cinema; however, it remains an open question whether this broad structural analogy alone can justify parallel comparison between the two cinemas. Throughout the book, the contiguous presentation of the three ‘Chinese’ cinemas often elides, rather than work through, these incomparables. Nevertheless, overall, Zhang’s trailblazing history of Chinese cinemas masterfully elucidates the mutual entanglement and resonances between mainland Chinese, Taiwanese, and Hong Kong cinemas.

title: Book Reviews of David Wang’s Fin-De-Sìecle Splendor: Repressed Modernities of Late Qing Fiction (1997) and The Transformation of the Narrative Pattern of Chinese Novels (Zhongguo xiaoshuo xushu moshi de zhuanbian) (1988)
text:
In this essay, I will be reviewing two highly influential monographs in the study of Chinese literary modernity: Chen Pingyuan’s The Transformation of the Narrative Pattern of Chinese Novels Zhongguo xiaoshuo xushu moshi de zhuanbian (1988) and David Wang’s Fin-De-Sìecle Splendor: Repressed Modernities of Late Qing Fiction (1997). Chen’s book studies the adoption of Western narrative techniques in late Qing new fiction and May Fourth fiction. Wang’s monograph presents the alternative trajectories of modernity that have been repressed in the standard literary historiography of modern Chinese fiction by studying neglected genres of late Qing fiction. The two writers emphasize two completely different aspects of Chinese literary modernity. Chen is primarily concerned with the transition between late Qing new fiction, which are often considered the earliest experiments with Western narrative modes, and the succeeding period of May Fourth fiction, which is the beginning of modern Chinese literature in standard literary histories. Whereas Chen focuses on indigenous transformations involved in the modernization of Chinese fiction culminating in May Fourth fiction, Wang argues against the prevailing May Fourth paradigm that suggests a singular path of literary modernization, and instead proposes to uncover “repressed modernities” in late Qing fiction, so as to open up the horizon of what it means for Chinese literature to be “modern.”(Wang 342) By drawing attention to the literary innovations of late Qing fiction, both writers expand the genealogy of Chinese literary modernity.
In Transformations, Chen studies the development of modern Chinese fiction along three narratological axes: time, perspective, and structure (Chen 4, 26). In chapter two, Chen studies how the translation and adaptation of Western political, mystery, and romance novels in late Qing new fiction introduced new narrative temporalities like inverted and discontinuous storytelling (50). Chen argues that these new narrative sequences started to move away from the linear natural time-order that characterized traditional Chinese fiction (Chen 52-3). By the May Fourth period, writers like Lu Xun and Chen Xianghe went even further from the traditional narrative sequence by experimenting with fragmented narrative sequences that defy linear causal order (Chen 62-3). Chapter three analyzes how the adoption of Western narrative perspectives like limited first-person and third-person narration gradually displaced the omniscient narration of traditional Chinese fiction. Chen shows how late Qing translations of Western mystery and adventure novels modified the originals’ first-person narration into the third person in order to aid the comprehension of readers (Chen 76). Although many new fiction writers adopted limited first-person narration in their travelogue fiction, the narrator merely served as a bystander that would retell past adventures or another character’s story (Chen 78, 80). Unlike new fiction writers, Chen argues that the use of first-person narration in May Fourth fiction foregrounded the interior subjectivity of the narrator (Chen 92). Chen emphasizes that May Fourth writers were more self-conscious in their adoption of limited first-person narration, thereby overcoming the inconsistences present in the new fiction writers’ earlier adaptations of first-person narration (Chen 95, 103). He briefly mentions the influence of the Japanese I-novel on Chinese writers, but, surprisingly, he does not further explore the Japanese connection in this or other sections of his book (Chen 98). In chapter four, Chen describes how modern Chinese fiction slowly moved away from the plot-centered structure of traditional Chinese fiction. He carefully studies new fiction writers’ literary innovations with regards to psychological interiority and landscape but concludes that the dominance of plot inherited from traditional fiction remains largely unchallenged until the May Fourth writers (Chen 121, 123). Citing writers like Lu Xun and Yu Dafu, Chen proposes that May Fourth fiction’s preoccupation with introspective feeling, monologues, and subconscious states evinces a common concern for individual expression, which displaces the centrality of plot in traditional Chinese fiction (Chen 126-8, 134-6).
Throughout his book, Chen studies the indigenous transformation of traditional Chinese fiction in the wider literary modernization context of emulating Western narrative techniques. On the one hand, Chen’s monograph contains meticulous studies of literary innovations in late Qing new fiction that begin to transform the narrative conventions of traditional Chinese fiction. On the other hand, Chen will usually end his discussion of new fiction by implying the limitations of these literary innovations in comparison to later May Fourth deployments of Western narrative technique. In other words, a linear scheme of literary modernization recurringly appears as a motif in Chen’s description of the transition between late Qing new fiction and May Fourth fiction. However, the richness of the literary innovations in new fiction that Chen himself describes appears to resist this type of schematization. After all, why should these innovations not be considered on their own merit, as opposed to being staged as lesser predecessors of later May Fourth developments? To be sure, Chen himself is quite aware of the difficulty of squaring the many diverse indigenous literary innovations and the genealogy of literary modernization. In chapters five, six, and seven, Chen shifts the focus to the internal transformations of the Chinese literary field (Chen 167). He analyzes how fiction moved from the margins to the center of the literary field, and, in the process, absorbed literary techniques from other classical genres such as anecdotes, comedies, travelogues, and diaries (Chen 203, 217).
In Fin-De-Siècle, Wang precisely argues against the linear teleological view of literary modernity that is adopted as a main hermeneutic framework by critics like Chen. Against the prevailing paradigm that crowns May Fourth fiction as the origin of modern Chinese novel, Wang analyzes late Qing fiction, not as a “prelude” to modern Chinese literature, but rather as a valuable repository of many possible literary modernities that were subsequently repressed in the polemics of the May Fourth movement (Wang 16). He explores these repressed aspects of Chinese literary modernity by studying the hitherto neglected genres of late Qing fiction: courtesan novel, grotesque exposé, chivalric and court-case tales, and science fantasy (Wang 50). In chapter two, Wang studies the edification of desire in late Qing courtesan novels, particularly how the representation of desire vacillates between excessive eroticization and moral containment of desire (Wang 59, 72). Chapter three argues that the late Qing chivalric and court-case tales explore the contingency and uncertainty of justice in a time of great social change (Wang 121). Wang analyzes how stories like The Travels of Lao Can and Living Hell subvert the conventions of the chivalric and court-case genre by meditating on the equivocity between justice and evil, as well as between law and violence (Wang 150, 180). Interestingly, in stark contrast to Chen’s high appraisal of May Fourth aesthetics, Wang suggests that the May Fourth writers’ harsh criticism of the allegedly conservative orientation of court-case and chivalric tales, and their inability to see the formal innovations in these works, reflect the intellectual poverty of May Fourth ideological polemics (Wang 121). Chapter four studies how the late Qing grotesque exposés reflect the crises in contemporary society in highly stylized manner, through “exaggeration, disfiguration, and metamorphosis.” (Wang 185) Wang argues that the carnivalesque world of these exposés display a playful engagement with the real that stands in stark contrast with the sober revolutionary realism of May Fourth writers (Wang 251). In chapter five, Wang proposes that late Qing science fantasy imagines “new ways of narrating the nation” by adopting new topoi from Western science fiction as well as transforming conventions from traditional Chinese writings on the fantastic (Wang 257-8). In his concluding chapter on reinterpreting contemporary Chinese fiction in light of these late Qing repressed modernities, Wang reminds the reader that he is not seeking to write a new literary history of the modern Chinese novel, but merely arguing for diversifying the interpretive horizon of modern Chinese literature to include more heterogeneous voices (Wang 341-2).
Even though Wang insists he is not offering a new origin or genealogy of modern Chinese literature, he ultimately expands the purview of the genealogy of modern Chinese fiction. In fact, Wang’s project can be understood as a continuation of the last three chapters of Chen’s monograph, namely the study of indigenous transformations of traditional Chinese fiction. Chen investigates the “silent revolution” taking place among late Qing writers at the turn of the 19th century to show that May Fourth literary innovations have their roots in earlier narrative experiments (Chen 32-3). Wang instead shifts the focus to late Qing texts throughout the second half of the 19th century beyond the canonical new fiction writers; in so doing, he questions the standard literary historiography of modern Chinese fiction and suggests a much more cacophonous picture of Chinese literary modernity. Written in the 1980s against the backdrop of Marxist literary historiography and European formalist narratologies, Chen’s innovative edge lies in his insistence on studying the narratological innovations of Chinese fiction without reducing these developments into social scientific models of cultural modernization or assuming one-to-one emulation of European narrative modes. Wang takes further the question of what makes the literary modernity of modern Chinese literature Chinese by speculating on the alternative paths of Chinese literary modernity. Ultimately, both monographs complicate and enrich our historical understanding of modern Chinese fiction by adopting more expansive views of Chinese literary modernity.

title: About
text: My name is Ezra Tandela (or 陈主荣 in Chinese). I am a PhD student in the Department of Comparative Literature at Harvard University. I work on the literary and cultural history of twentieth century in East Asia. My ongoing interests include: the history of the decolonial movement among Asian creatives from the 1950s to the 1970s, the transmission of Confucian classics in education broadcasts of post-war Japan, and travel writing in early twentieth century East Asia.
